text: To filter a photo with Warp, you open it with {{c1::PIL}}, turn it into a {{c2::NumPy}} float32 array, upload it with wp.array, launch the kernel, call .numpy() on the output, and save it with Image.fromarray.
extra: NumPy sits in the middle both ways. PIL to NumPy to Warp on the way in, and Warp to NumPy to PIL on the way out.

text: Check image.mode first. Mode L is greyscale with NumPy shape {{c1::(h, w)}}. RGB has shape {{c2::(h, w, 3)}}, and RGBA has shape {{c3::(h, w, 4)}}.
extra: Each channel stores one 8-bit unsigned value per pixel.

text: Pillow's image.size gives {{c1::(w, h)}}, but the NumPy array is {{c2::(h, w, c)}}. Reshape greyscale to {{c3::(h, w, 1)}} so one 3D kernel handles every mode.
extra: Remove that extra axis again before saving a mode L image, because PIL will not build greyscale from shape (h, w, 1).

text: On an RGBA image you filter only the channels where {{c1::k < 3}} and {{c2::copy the alpha}} channel unchanged. If alpha stays at zero from wp.zeros, you save a fully {{c3::transparent}} image.
extra: Filtering transparency makes no sense. On a fully opaque test image the bug can look fine, so it is easy to miss.

text: In Docker on a laptop, you set the Warp device to {{c1::"cpu"}}. On an Nvidia GPU or in Colab, you set it to {{c2::"cuda"}}.
extra: cpu is the portable serial fallback. cuda runs the kernel in parallel on the GPU.

text: You upload the image with wp.array and allocate the output with {{c1::\(\text{wp.zeros\_like}\) }}, so it gets the same shape, dtype, and device, filled with {{c2::zeros}}.
extra: On cuda, wp.array copies the host data onto the GPU. The study guide also accepts wp.zeros with an explicit shape.

text: To pass a filter radius or an unsharp \(k\) into a kernel, you add it as a {{c1::typed argument}}. Warp reads the value at {{c2::launch}}, so you can change it without recompiling.
extra: Put the type in the kernel signature, then pass the number in inputs= with the arrays.
